summary: This work demonstrates magnetic flux trapping suppression in superconducting circuits using on-chip resistive heaters that generate thermal gradients to drive vortices toward moats (etched holes) during cooldown in ambient magnetic fields $B_r \leq 60$ µT. Magnetic imaging with NV-diamond microscopy and electrical measurements of Josephson junction chains confirm effective flux removal both during field cooling and from circuit-generated vortices.
motivation: Magnetic flux trapping in superconducting thin films (Nb, NbN, NbTiN, Al, Ta) degrades qubit coherence and digital circuit performance, with a single vortex capable of disrupting device operation; scaling to large circuits exacerbates this problem as trapped vortex number scales as $N_{\Phi_0} = B_r A / \Phi_0$, making a practical defluxing solution necessary.
method: Mo resistors (40 nm thick, 1 µm wide, $\sim$2 Ω/□) in the SFQ5ee process create localized thermal gradients ($\lesssim 50$ mK/µm) that drive vortices toward moat-containing ground planes (M1, M4, M7 Nb layers with 10 µm square moats spaced 10 µm apart) during cooldown via thermal force $F_{\mathrm{th}} \propto \nabla T$ that overcomes pinning forces near $T_c$; flux distribution and circuit performance monitored via widefield magnetic imaging and critical current measurements of JJ chains.
result: At $B_r = 63.6$ µT with $\dot{Q} = 0.78$ mW applied to outer moat resistors during cooldown, vortices are completely expelled from the film between heaters and concentrate in aligned moats; electrical recovery of suppressed JJ chains shows $>99\%$ of junctions restore baseline behavior at $\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{max}} \geq 4.26$ mW (corresponding to $\Delta T \approx 9.2$ K and $|\nabla T| \approx 44$ mK/µm), with up to $8\Phi_0$ trapped per moat demonstrating capability to suppress flux over large-scale circuits with basic magnetic shielding.
